events.title: The Second Council of Constantinople opens
events.shortBlurb: Justinian summoned the fifth ecumenical council to condemn the Three Chapters, and Pope Vigilius, a prisoner in all but name, refused to attend…
body: On 5 May 553 the Second Council of Constantinople, reckoned the fifth ecumenical council, opened in the imperial city, called together by the Emperor Justinian. Nearly all its fathers were bishops of the East — only six came out of the Latin West, and those Africans; the presidency fell to Eutychius, patriarch of the city.

At issue were the Three Chapters: the person and writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia, certain writings of Theodoret of Cyrus against St. Cyril of Alexandria, and the letter of Ibas of Edessa. Pope Vigilius, detained in Constantinople since 547, had once condemned the chapters in his Judicatum of 548 and then withdrawn it under Western protest; he would not sit in a council where Eastern prelates so outnumbered his own.

In eight sessions the bishops heard the chapters read and, on 2 June, the 165 present condemned them in fourteen anathemas, while Justinian struck the pope's name from the diptychs. Vigilius, exiled for a season, yielded at last and condemned the chapters himself, in December 553 and again in February 554; but the West was slow to follow — Milan and Aquileia broke communion with Rome, and the schism of Aquileia endured nearly to the year 700.
